Skunks are one of Georgia's primary rabies carriers, so a skunk denning against an occupied Jenkinsburg home is a genuine public-health concern — never approach, corner, or handle a skunk or disturb an active den. Beyond rabies, skunk spray is a respiratory and eye irritant, skunks dig up lawns foraging for grubs, and they can damage foundation skirting and crawlspace vapor barriers while denning. Any bite or scratch from a skunk, or a pet's close encounter with one, should be treated as a possible rabies exposure.

faqs.q: There's a skunk denning under my Jenkinsburg deck — what should I do?
faqs.a: Under decks, porches, sheds, outbuildings, and foundations are the classic Jenkinsburg skunk den sites. Timing matters most: from roughly February through May, females are raising non-mobile kits, and sealing or trapping out the mother strands the young to die under the structure — a worse odor and contamination problem than the skunk itself. Outside kit season, a licensed contractor will use gentle eviction or a humane trap and then install buried 1/4-inch hardware-cloth exclusion so nothing can re-den there. DIY attempts risk a spray event that drives odor into the structure.

faqs.q: What time of year do skunks have kits in Jenkinsburg?
faqs.a: Female skunks select den sites in late winter and give birth in spring — kits are typically present from roughly February through May and stay in the den until they are weaned and mobile, about 8-10 weeks. That spring window is exactly when exclusion has to be handled carefully so kits aren't sealed inside. Skunks stay active year-round in central Georgia's mild climate, but spring denning and fall foraging drive the heaviest Jenkinsburg call volume.

faqs.q: How do I get rid of skunk smell — does tomato juice work?
faqs.a: Skip the tomato juice — it only masks the odor. Skunk spray is an oily thiol compound that has to be chemically broken down, not covered up. Effective cleanup uses an enzymatic deodorizer (or, for pets and small surfaces, a fresh peroxide, baking-soda, and dish-soap mix); for spray that has soaked into a deck, crawlspace, or the area under a structure, professional enzyme treatment of the contaminated material is what actually removes the smell. Removing the skunk and sealing the den first is essential — deodorizing while a skunk is still present just resets the next day.

snake-removal.extendedBody:
What Snakes Actually Live Around Jenkinsburg

Central Georgia's snake reality is far narrower than the full Southeast venomous roster homeowners often fear. Around Jenkinsburg, the copperhead is the primary venomous concern — it favors wooded creek corridors, leaf litter, and the brushy edges of rural-acreage lots, where it hunts rodents and is easy to step near because of its camouflage. Timber rattlesnakes occur in the area's wooded tracts at low density and are encountered far less often. Cottonmouths are limited to the immediate edge of water — pond banks and creek margins — and are not a general yard snake on Jenkinsburg properties; most "moccasin" sightings away from water are harmless watersnakes.

The vast majority of Jenkinsburg snake calls are non-venomous — eastern rat snakes, black racers, watersnakes, and hognose snakes. These species are beneficial rodent and pest controllers and are routinely killed by mistake because they get confused for copperheads. Jenkinsburg's pine-hardwood remnants, surrounding agricultural land, and rural-acreage lots with outbuildings concentrate both the rodent prey and the cover that draw all of these snakes toward homes.

Snake in Your House or Garage? What to Do Right Now

If a snake is inside your Jenkinsburg home or garage, the safest response is also the simplest:

  • Do not approach or try to handle it. Most bites happen when people corner, kill, or pick up a snake — even a non-venomous one can bite.
  • Keep it in sight from a safe distance. Watching where it is lets the technician find and remove it quickly; a snake that slips into a wall or a cluttered garage is much harder to recover.
  • Confine the room if you can. Close interior doors or block the gap under the door with a towel to keep the snake in one space.
  • Keep children and pets well away until the snake is removed.
  • Call for professional identification and removal. Never try to ID a snake up close — let a licensed pro confirm the species from a safe distance and relocate it.

How to Keep Snakes Away From Your Jenkinsburg Property

Snakes follow food and cover, so the durable fixes target both:

  • Control rodents first. A mouse or rat problem is the single biggest snake attractant. Secure feed, pet food, and trash, and address rodent harborage in barns and sheds — snakes leave when the prey does.
  • Cut the cover. Clear woodpiles, brush, leaf litter, tall grass, and dense ground cover back from the house, and keep firewood stacked off the ground and away from the foundation.
  • Seal the gaps. Snakes enter through openings as small as a quarter inch — foundation cracks, weep holes, gaps under doors, and pipe or HVAC penetrations. Sealing these keeps snakes, and the rodents they follow, out.

On Jenkinsburg's rural-acreage properties, the heaviest snake pressure comes from outbuildings and woodpiles — barns, equipment sheds, and stacked wood give both rodents and snakes harborage right next to where people live and work. Whole-property attention to rodents and cover, not just the main residence, is what keeps snake encounters down. Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division regulations apply to snake handling and relocation in Butts County.

Rural-acreage properties with multiple outbuildings and woodpile harborage run toward the higher end. Call for an estimate.

faqs.a: Around Jenkinsburg the copperhead is the primary venomous concern — it favors wooded creek corridors and the brushy edges of rural-acreage lots. Timber rattlesnakes occur in wooded areas at low density and are seen far less often. Cottonmouths stay at the immediate edge of water (pond banks, creek margins) and are not a general yard snake here — most "moccasins" people report away from water are harmless watersnakes. The vast majority of local snakes are non-venomous and beneficial — eastern rat snakes, black racers, watersnakes, and hognose. Never approach a snake to identify it; if you can't confirm it from a safe distance, treat it as venomous and call a licensed professional.

faqs.q: Why are snakes coming onto my Jenkinsburg property?
faqs.a: Snakes follow their food supply. A Jenkinsburg property with a mouse or rat problem will attract snakes, and rural-acreage barns, sheds, and feed storage are common rodent — and therefore snake — magnets. Dense ground cover, woodpiles, and tall grass provide shelter and hunting ground. Eliminating rodent harborage is the most effective long-term snake deterrent, alongside physical exclusion of structures.

faqs.q: Can snakes get inside my Jenkinsburg house?
faqs.a: Yes. Snakes can enter through gaps as small as a quarter inch — under exterior doors, around pipe and HVAC line penetrations, foundation cracks, weep holes, dryer-vent terminations, and unscreened crawl-space and gable vents. Most in-house snake calls are non-venomous rodent hunters that followed mice or rats through the same gap. A professional inspection identifies every ground-level entry point and seals them permanently with steel mesh, sealant, or appropriate door sweeps.

faqs.q: When are snakes most active around Jenkinsburg?
faqs.a: Snakes are most active in central Georgia from March through October. Spring emergence is the first peak — snakes come out of winter dormancy, bask in sunny areas, and move onto properties as temperatures warm. Fall is the second peak as snakes move toward winter den sites and occasionally enter structures seeking warmth. Jenkinsburg residents should be most cautious during these two transition periods.

opossum-removal.extendedBody:
Opossums in Jenkinsburg & Central Georgia

The Virginia opossum is common throughout central Georgia, and unlike opossums in colder regions it breeds in the Jenkinsburg area essentially year-round, with two main litters (roughly January through April, then June through August). Because of that long breeding season, opossums turn up in and around Jenkinsburg homes in every month of the year.

Jenkinsburg's setting drives the pattern. The rural-acreage lots and pine-hardwood remnants along the I-75 corridor in northern Butts County offer the cover and ground-level shelter opossums prefer — and the part of a Jenkinsburg property that draws them is almost always at or below grade: crawlspaces, the space under a deck or porch, and outbuildings such as barns, sheds, and equipment buildings. In summer, juveniles strike out on their own and disperse into garages, sheds, and under-deck spaces, which is when many Jenkinsburg calls come in. Opossums are nomadic opportunists rather than territorial nesters, so the same crawlspace or under-deck void is often used by a succession of different animals over time unless the opening is sealed.

The Case for Leaving Yard Opossums in Place

Not every opossum is a problem, and an opossum simply passing through the yard is usually worth leaving alone. Opossums are genuinely useful neighbors:

  • They very rarely carry rabies. An opossum's low body temperature makes it a poor host for the rabies virus, so opossums are among the least likely mammals in Georgia to transmit it.
  • They eat large numbers of ticks. Opossums groom constantly and consume the ticks they find, removing many from the local environment each season — a real benefit on tick-heavy rural Jenkinsburg lots.
  • They prey on rodents and pests. Opossums eat mice, rats, insects, snails, and carrion, helping hold down the same rodent populations that draw in snakes and other wildlife.

A yard-only opossum, with no den under a structure, will usually move on within two to four weeks on its own. The opossums that do warrant action are the ones that have moved under a deck, into a crawlspace, an attic, or an outbuilding — those should be excluded, and any droppings cleaned up, because a sheltered den gets reused and can become a sanitation problem. The practical rule for Jenkinsburg: exclude the under-structure animals, and let the harmless yard visitors move along.

How to Keep Opossums Out From Under Your Jenkinsburg Deck or Crawlspace

The fact that makes opossum prevention straightforward: opossums do not dig. They use openings that already exist, so closing those openings keeps them out for good.

  • Seal crawlspace vents and skirting gaps. Close unscreened or broken crawlspace vents and gaps in deck and porch skirting with 1/4-inch hardware cloth buried several inches into the soil and bent outward in an L-footer — that also stops the animals that actually do dig.
  • Secure food sources. Keep trash-can lids latched, bring pet food indoors at night, and clean up fallen fruit and spilled birdseed — the easy meals that draw opossums onto a property in the first place.
  • Remove under-deck and outbuilding harborage. Clear the leaf piles, scrap wood, and debris that collect under decks and along barns, sheds, and equipment buildings, and close off the dark, sheltered voids opossums den in.
  • Confirm the space is empty first. Never seal a crawlspace or under-deck opening until you are certain no animal — especially a female with pouch young — is inside, or it will be trapped in. A licensed contractor verifies the space is clear before sealing.

All trapping and removal is handled under licensed, humane practice through the Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division.

Because opossums are nomadic and opportunistic, several different animals may use the same opening over time, so trapping one without sealing the access just leaves the spot open for the next. Permanent sealing of every ground-level opening is the only lasting fix.
